text: Two halves. First the common-mode feedback of Lectures 10 to 12, with every C M F B question. Then speed: how fast an op amp’s output can move.
Speed needs frequency, poles and bandwidth. You have not met those yet, so a whole chapter builds them from zero, a capacitor, a time constant, a sine wave, before Lecture 13 uses them.
Every theory chapter ends with its questions, and every question stops for your answer before it is explained.
Your page starts with an identity that is always true: each input is the average of the two (the common mode) plus half the difference.
The C M part is the same in both. The D M part has equal size and opposite sign. Nothing else is needed to describe two signals.
Picture it: two sine waves moving in opposite directions around a shared level. That shared level is V C M; the swinging part is the differential signal.
Change only the C M and both waves slide up together; the difference does not change. Change only the D M and they move further apart; the average stays put.
Why we care: at the outputs, the differential part is our signal. The common part, the outputs’ shared D C level, is not controlled by anything yet.
Lecture 9 showed what goes wrong: with current-source loads the output C M is set by a tiny current mismatch times a huge resistance. Lecture 10 builds the loop that fixes it.
C M is V 1 plus V 2 over 2, D M is V 1 minus V 2. D M moves the outputs apart, C M moves them together.

Before the C M F B loop, follow the currents in the amplifier it controls. Two rules: in an N mos, current flows from drain to source, downwards. And current never chooses a path: the sources set it, the devices share it.
Start at the bottom. The tail source pulls I S S out of node P, where the sources of M 1 and M 2 meet, and sends it to ground.
That current reaches P through M 1 and M 2. K C L at P: I S S equals I D 1 plus I D 2. With equal inputs the pair is symmetric, so each side carries half, I S S over 2.
At the top, each load source pushes I 1 down from V D D into its output node.

K C L at each output: I 1 comes in and I D 1 goes out, so they must be equal. But two separate sources set them. Any mismatch has nowhere to go except the node’s huge resistance: that is the Lecture 9 drift.
That is the C M F B amplifier’s job: it trims the tail until I S S equals 2 I 1 exactly. Then both output nodes balance and nothing drifts.
Now a small differential input: V in 1 up a little, V in 2 down. M 1 takes delta I more, M 2 gives up the same delta I. The total is still I S S: the tail does not care how it is shared.
M 1 pulls delta I more than its load gives, so V out 1 falls; V out 2 rises by the same amount. The average does not move, so the C M F B loop sees nothing.
The current rules for this pair, in one card. Sources set the currents; K C L at each node tells you how they split.
Example: each load source gives I 1 equals 0.5 milliamps. For neither output to drift, how much current must the tail carry?

With this differential input, M 1 carries I S S over 2 plus delta I and M 2 carries I S S over 2 minus delta I, while each load still gives exactly I 1 equals I S S over 2. What do the two outputs do?
Your page’s general structure. The pair M 1, M 2 with current-source loads I 1, the amplifier whose output C M floats.
Block 1, the C M sensing circuit: takes V out 1 and V out 2 and produces their average, V out, C M, ignoring the differential signal.
Block 2, the C M F B amplifier: compares V out, C M with a reference V ref, the level we want.
Block 3, the correction: its output adjusts one current source, here the tail I S S.
Follow the loop. Suppose the outputs drift up: V out, C M exceeds V ref,
the C M F B amplifier’s output rises,
the tail pulls more current,
and both outputs are pulled back down. Negative feedback: it settles where V out, C M equals V ref.
Key point: the differential signal leaves the average unchanged, so the C M F B loop never fights the signal. It only fixes the shared level.
C M F B: sense V out, C M, compare with V ref, correct a current source.
The same pair, now with P mos loads M 3 and M 4 and two sensing resistors between the outputs. Follow the bias currents first, then the resistor current.
Bias first. The tail pulls I S S out of node P. M 3 and M 4 each push I S S over 2 down from V D D, straight through M 1 and M 2. P mos: source to drain. N mos: drain to source. Both downwards.
At rest both outputs sit at the same voltage. No voltage across R 1 and R 2 means no current in them.
Now a differential output: V out 1 up, V out 2 down. A current I R flows from the higher output, through R 1 and R 2, into the lower one. The midpoint stays at the average.

Where does I R come from? K C L at V out 1: M 3’s current now feeds both M 1 and the resistor. The resistor takes signal current away from the output node. That is the gain loss: R 1 appears in parallel with R O.
In common mode the midpoint rises with the outputs, so no extra current flows. The sensing resistors carry only the differential current.
The current rules for resistive sensing: bias currents go down, the resistor current goes across, and only for a differential signal.
Example: V out 1 equals 1.0 volt, V out 2 equals 0.8 volts, R 1 equals R 2 equals 10 kilo-ohms. How much current flows through the sensing resistors?
Now both outputs rise by 50 millivolts together (a pure C M change), with R 1 equals R 2 equals 10 kilo-ohms. What change of current flows in R 1?
The simplest C M sensor: two resistors R 1 equals R 2 in series between the outputs. Their midpoint is the C M.
Why the midpoint is the average, superposition (your page). Keep only V out 1 (set V out 2 to 0): a divider gives V out 1 R 2 over ( R 1 plus R 2 ).
Keep only V out 2: V out 2 R 1 over ( R 1 plus R 2 ).
Add them; with R 1 equals R 2 every factor is ½: exactly the average.
The cost: for the differential signal the midpoint is AC ground, so each output now has R 1 hanging on it, in parallel with R O 1 in parallel with R O 3.
Unless R 1 is far bigger than R O (megohms), the gain drops. That is why Tutorial 5 Q 3 uses R equals 10 mega-ohms, and still loses a little.
The fix on your page: put a source follower between each output and its resistor, so the resistors never touch the high-resistance outputs.
V out, C M equals V out 1 plus V out 2 2.
The cost: A. V equals G M 1 ( R O 1 in parallel with R O 3 in parallel with R 1 ).
The follower sensor. Three separate groups of current live here: the main pair, follower M 5 with I 1, and follower M 6 with I 2.
The followers carry their own bias. I 1 flows from V D D down through M 5, drain to source, into its current source. I 2 does the same through M 6.
The main pair is unchanged: I S S in the tail, half down each side. The outputs touch only the followers’ gates, and a gate takes no current, so these groups never mix.
Now a differential signal: M 5’s source goes up, M 6’s goes down. A current I R flows out of M 5’s source, through R 1 and R 2, into M 6’s source.
K C L at M 5’s source: M 5 now supplies I 1 plus I R, and M 6 supplies I R less. The followers deliver the resistor current.
So the outputs keep their full resistance and the gain is untouched. Only the followers work harder.
The current rules for follower sensing: each follower carries its own bias, and the resistor current comes from the followers, never from the outputs.

Example: I 1 equals I 2 equals 20 microamps and R 1 equals R 2 equals 50 kilo-ohms. A differential signal puts M 5’s source at 0.6 volts and M 6’s source at 0.4 volts. How much current does M 5 carry now? First, step 1. First: how much current I R flows through R 1 and R 2?
How much of the resistor current I R comes out of the amplifier’s output nodes (the M 1, M 3 drains)?
Your page’s second sensor: each output drives the gate of a source follower (M 5, M 6, biased by I 1, I 2 ). The resistors hang on the followers’ sources instead.
Why it works: a gate draws no current, so the outputs see nothing extra, their high resistance (and the gain) is untouched.
The price: a follower’s source sits one link below its gate. Your page’s numbers: outputs at 0.9 volts, follower sources at 0.5 volts.
So the sensed value is the average shifted down by V G S 5, 6, choose V ref (or the amplifier’s other input) to match.
Your page also marks each follower output as D C + AC: the C M level plus the signal. Averaging cancels the signal and keeps the level.
One more cost to remember (Lecture 10 handout): the outputs are now follower gates, so they cannot go below about V G S plus V overdrive, the followers eat some swing.
Follower sensing: V sense equals V out, C M minus V G S, no loading, some swing lost.

The Quiz 2 circuit. Start at the reference: 50 microamps flows from V D D down through diode M 6 into the current source.
M 3 and M 4 have the same W over L and the same gate voltage as M 6, so each copies 50 microamps. Each copy flows straight down through its input transistor, M 1 or M 2, into node P.
K C L at P: M 5 must pull exactly 100 microamps. Nothing copies that number into M 5. The C M F B amplifier moves M 5’s gate until it does.

Suppose M 5 pulled 110 microamps. The loads still give only 100 microamps, so the extra 10 microamps is drawn out of the output nodes and both outputs fall. The amplifier sees V O, C M below V ref and lowers M 5’s gate until the tail is back to 100 microamps.
A differential input only re-shares: M 1 takes 50 microamps plus delta I, M 2 takes 50 microamps minus delta I, and the tail still sees 100 microamps.
The current rules for this circuit: the mirrors fix the loads, K C L fixes the tail, and the C M F B amplifier makes M 5 obey it.

In this circuit the reference is 50 microamps and (W over L) 3 equals (W over L) 4 equals (W over L) 6. With the outputs at rest (no current in the R’s), how much current must the tail M 5 carry? First, step 1. First: how much current does M 3 carry?

What it tests: turning a gain into an overdrive ( A. D equals 1 over ( lambda V overdrive ) ), the output range from checks (its middle is V ref ), the input-C M range from a check + a fence, and what ±1 percent means for the C M gain.

The trick: with equal lambda, R O 1 in parallel with R O 3 equals 1 over (2 lambda I D ) and G M equals 2 I D over V overdrive, so the current cancels: A. D equals 1 over ( lambda V overdrive 1 ), giving V overdrive 1 equals 0.1 volts, V overdrive 5 equals 0.2 volts, V overdrive 3 equals 0.3 volts.
Lowest output: the tail’s and M 1’s overdrives, 0.3 volts. Highest: 1.8 minus 0.3 equals 1.5 volts. C M F B holds the C M at V ref, so put it in the middle: 0.9 volts.

Floor: tail check plus the link up to M 1’s gate, 0.2 plus 0.5 equals 0.7 volts. Ceiling: M 1’s drain sits at V O, C M equals 0.9 volts and its gate may be V threshold above: 1.3 volts. The middle, 1.0 volt, is the optimum.
C M gain equals output-C M change divided by input-C M change: (2 times 0.01 times 0.9) over 0.6 equals 0.03. The C M F B loop must make the C M gain at least this small.

Pattern for C M F B level questions: overdrives first, output range by checks (middle equals V ref ), input range by check + link and fence (middle equals optimum), then C M gain equals allowed change divided by input range.

The 2024 mid sem circuit, with I 1 equals 50 microamps, I 2 equals 200 microamps and W over L equals 50 for every device. The main amplifier is the Quiz circuit again: M 3 and M 4 copy 50 microamps, so the tail M 5 carries 100 microamps. Now follow the error amplifier on the right.

In the error amplifier, I 2 equals 200 microamps flows down through diode M 12. M 11 has the same W over L and gate voltage, so it copies 200 microamps and feeds the joined sources of the P mos pair M 7, M 8.
K C L at the pair’s sources: the 200 microamps splits. With V O, C M equals V ref the gates are equal, so 100 microamps goes down each side, into the diodes M 9 and M 10.
Diode M 9 and the tail M 5 share a gate voltage and have the same W over L, so M 5 copies M 9’s 100 microamps. That is exactly the 100 microamps the main amplifier needs: the loop is balanced.
V O, C M going up makes M 8 conduct less, so M 7 takes the extra share. M 9’s current rises, M 5 copies it and pulls harder, and both outputs come back down. Negative feedback.
The current rules for this C M F B circuit: each mirror copies its reference, the error pair re-shares a fixed 200 microamps, and M 5 copies M 7’s share.
At balance ( V O, C M equals V ref ), how much current flows in M 7? ( I 2 equals 200 microamps, all W over L equals 50.) First, step 1. First: how much current does M 11 carry?
The output C M drifts up, above V ref ( V O, C M drives M 8’s gate). How does the 200 microamps from M 11 re-split, and what does the tail do?

The Tutorial 5 Q 2 folded cascode. Two P mos sources at the top each push I P down from V D D into a folding node.
The input pair hangs from those nodes. The tail pulls I S S, and with equal inputs M 1 and M 2 each take I S S over 2, out of the left and the right folding node.
K C L at the left folding node: I P comes in, and leaves either through M 1 or down the cascode branch.

The rest, I P minus I S S over 2, folds down through the P mos cascode, the output node and the N mos cascode into M 3. M 3 must sink exactly that, and its gate is V E: the C M F B amplifier makes it match.

With a differential input each cascode branch changes opposite to its input transistor. M 3 and M 4 do not change, so the difference flows out of one output and into the other. The outputs move apart; the C M stays.
The current rules for the folded cascode: the top source current folds, part into the input pair and the rest down the cascode, and the C M F B sets the bottom sinks to match.

Example numbers (Tutorial 5 Q 2 gives none): each top P mos source gives I P equals 1 milliamp and the tail gives I S S equals 1 milliamp, with equal inputs. How much current flows down each cascode branch into M 3 and M 4? First, step 1. First: how much current does the input transistor M 1 carry?

What it tests: Lecture 9’s habit of matching an amplifier to the levels around it, and the C M loop gain read as sense, then amplify, then current, then resistance.

Levels decide it. V E must sit near V G S 3, close to ground. A P mos input pair has its N mos mirror at the bottom, so its output rests near V G S, N, the right level. An N mos pair’s output would rest near V D D minus V G S, P.
Break the loop and follow a C M change: the sensor passes it with gain 1, the error amp multiplies by A. E A., M 3, M 4 turn it into G M 3 A. E A. times that current,
and that current lands on each output, which (for a C M change) sees only the cascodes: R up in parallel with R down. Loop gain T equals A. E A. G M 3 ( R up in parallel with R down ).
Check the sign too: V out, C M up, then V E up, then M 3, M 4 pull harder, then outputs down. Negative feedback, as required.
The error amplifier is a differential pair with a current-mirror load, and its output V E drives the gates of M 3 and M 4. Should its input pair be P mos or N mos?

The triode equation (your page). Now make V D S tiny, tens of millivolts.
Then V D S squared is negligible next to 2( V G S minus V threshold ) V D S: drop it. The current is proportional to V D S.
A current proportional to the voltage is a resistor: R on equals 1 over ( mu n C ox W over L ( V G S minus V threshold )).
On the I D, V D S curves (your sketch): near the origin each curve is a straight line through zero. Its slope is 1 over R on.
Zoom in: every curve is a line. A bigger V G S gives a steeper line, a smaller resistance. The gate controls the resistance.
Your page’s one-liner: in saturation a MOSFET is a voltage-controlled current source; in deep triode it is a voltage-controlled resistor. Lectures 11 to 12 use the resistor.
R on equals 1 over ( mu n C ox W over L ( V G S minus V threshold )).
Let us follow the current in Lecture 11’s telescopic, with the numbers of Tutorial 5 Question 1: each column carries half a milliamp.

Start at the top. M 8 and M 9 have a fixed gate bias, so they are current sources: each pushes half a milliamp down its own column. A P mos conducts from its source at the supply to its drain, so the current flows down.
Nothing leaves the column on the way down. The same current passes the output node, then the N mos cascode and the input device. An N mos conducts from drain to source: down again.
The blue wires from the outputs to the gates of M 10 and M 11 carry a voltage, not a current: a gate draws no current.
At node P the two columns meet. Kirchhoff’s current law: whatever flows into P must flow out, and the only way out is down through the triode devices M 10 and M 11.
One milliamp arrives at P. With equal outputs, M 10 and M 11 are equal resistors, so they split it equally: half a milliamp each, down to ground.
Now add a small differential input: the input device M 2 takes a little more, I D plus delta I, and M 3 a little less, I D minus delta I.
Add them at P: plus delta I and minus delta I cancel. The total stays at one milliamp; the input only moves current from one side to the other.

But the P mos source on top still gives exactly I D. The extra delta I on the left has to come out of the output node, so V out 1 falls, and on the right V out 2 rises. That current mismatch is the output signal.
And the tail? V out 1 down makes M 10 a bigger resistor, V out 2 up makes M 11 a smaller one: the split under P shifts, but the sum still matches one milliamp.
Both outputs sit at the same voltage, and each column carries I D equals 0.5 milliamps. How much current flows from P to ground through M 10 and M 11 together?
With this small differential input, what happens to the total current flowing from P to ground?
Your page’s circuit: a telescopic op amp whose tail is two transistors M 10, M 11 in deep triode, with their gates driven by the two outputs.
They sit between node P and ground with only a tiny V D S (equals V P ), so each is a resistor set by its gate, that is, by an output voltage.
In parallel, conductances add: 1 over R total equals 1 over R on 10 plus 1 over R on 11,
each conductance is mu n C ox W over L ( V G S minus V threshold ) with V G S equals an output,
so only the sum V out 1 plus V out 2 appears, twice the output C M.
Watch the conductances. A differential signal raises one output and lowers the other: G10 grows, G11 shrinks by the same amount, the total does not move. The sensor ignores the signal.
A common-mode rise raises both: the total conductance grows, R total falls, the tail pulls harder, and the outputs are pulled back down. Feedback, built right into the tail.
R total equals 1 over ( mu n C ox W over L ( V out 1 plus V out 2 minus 2 V threshold )): sees C M, blind to D M.
Follow the current in the pair sensor. Two sources set everything: M 5 at the top, and the two sinks I 1 at the bottom. Take M 5 as 20 microamps and each sink as 50.
M 5 is a P mos with a fixed gate bias: a current source. Its 20 microamps flow down from the supply, source to drain, into the node below it.

At that node it splits: part goes down through M 3, the rest through M 4. K C L: I 5 equals I D 3 plus I D 4. With equal outputs the circuit is symmetric, so the halves are equal. When the outputs move away from V REF, the split shifts with the square of the difference: that shift is what the sensor measures.
Each follower carries its own current from the supply, drain to source. At the follower’s source node it meets M 3’s current, and the sink below takes both: I 1 equals I D 1 plus I D 3.
M 3 gets 10 microamps, so the follower M 1 carries the rest of the sink: 50 minus 10, 40 microamps. The same on the right.
The rule for every node: the sources set the currents, the devices only share them. If M 3 takes more, M 1 must take less, because the sink below is fixed.

The outputs are equal. M 5 supplies I 5 equals 20 microamps and each sink is I 1 equals 50 microamps. How much current flows through the follower M 1? First, step 1. How much of M 5’s current flows through M 3?
Another sensor on your page: followers M 1, M 2 copy the outputs, and P mos devices M 3, M 4 (gates at V ref ) compare them, sharing the current source M 5.
Each device’s current follows the square law of its own difference from V ref, so the sensed current is a sum of squares (your page’s last line).
And a sum of squares does not depend only on the sum of the outputs: for big swings the differential signal leaks into the reading. Good for small swings only.
Compare the triode sensor, whose reading depends exactly on V out 1 plus V out 2 (as long as the devices stay in deep triode).
Pair sensing: I grows like ( V ref minus V out 1 ) squared plus ( V ref minus V out 2 ) squared, nonlinear, small swings only.
Your page writes Lecture 1’s two lines again: the closed-loop result A. over (1 plus beta A.) and the error is about 1 over ( beta A.) (circled).
The C M F B loop is an ordinary negative-feedback loop. How close the output C M gets to V ref depends on its loop gain, just like the gain error of Lecture 1.
Your two circuits: an error amplifier comparing the resistor-sensed C M with V ref and driving a current source; or triode devices that sense and correct in one go.
Lecture 12 adds that the error amplifier can drive any current source in the output path, the input tail, or the bottom sources. Wherever it acts, it moves a current until V out, C M equals V ref.

Link: node P is M 3’s source, one V G S 3 below its gate: V P equals V B 1 minus V G S 3. The bias fixes P.
Ohm’s law: the whole tail current 2 I D flows through R total, P, so V P equals 2 I D R total, P.

and solve for V out 1 plus V out 2: the output C M is now fixed by sizes and biases. Questions use it both ways: size W over L for a wanted C M, or find the C M from the sizes.

Follow the current in the replica circuit. Take the source on the left as I 1 equals 100 microamps.
Start on the left, the replica branch. The source pushes I 1 down through M 14 and M 15 to ground. M 14 is diode-connected: its gate settles at whatever voltage lets it carry I 1.
